Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

vignette:
Aleksander Nowak is a 25-year-old Polish-American man who works as a salesperson at a home appliances showroom in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He came to the intake appointment wearing a pressed shirt and speaking carefully, as though choosing each word before releasing it. He has been in a relationship for two years, and his partner, he said quietly, was the one who finally persuaded him to come.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Aleksander was visiting extended family in a region of Eastern Europe that had, in the weeks before his arrival, become the edge of an active conflict zone. What had been described to him as a brief family visit - a few days, a summer table, his grandmother's cooking - became something else entirely when shelling began in the town on his third night there. He described lying on the floor of his grandmother's house with his cousins while the windows shook and a neighbour's structure collapsed in a sound he said was less like an explosion and more like the world folding in on itself. The family spent the following thirty-six hours sheltering in a basement with no reliable information about whether they would be able to leave. When they were eventually evacuated in a convoy, Aleksander watched through the vehicle window as parts of the town he had visited as a child were simply gone - walls standing without buildings behind them, a playground reduced to twisted metal. He returned to the United States ten days later, physically unharmed.

In the months that followed, Aleksander found himself carrying feelings he had no ready framework for. There was fear that arrived without warning - sharp, physical, and disproportionate to whatever was in front of him at the time. There was horror that seemed to attach itself to ordinary moments. And there was a persistent, grinding anger that he struggled to locate or direct, accompanied by a shame he found harder still to articulate: a sense that he had been helpless, that he had not done enough for his family, that something about him had been permanently exposed. These feelings did not diminish with time. If anything, they settled more deeply into him.

The nights became their own particular difficulty. Once darkness fell, Aleksander found that the sense of safety he could approximate during the day dissolved almost entirely. He would lie awake listening to the sounds of the street outside - a car backfiring, neighbours on a balcony, the distant rhythm of music - and find himself unable to locate himself in the present. What frightened him most, he said, was not any specific sound but the quality of darkness itself, the way it returned him to the basement and the shaking windows in a way daylight did not. He had come to believe that nighttime was simply when the world became less predictable, less containable, and he had no counter-evidence to offer himself.

At work, Aleksander's difficulties became concrete and consequential. His role requires him to hold extended conversations with customers, to track specifications, to remember what a client said twenty minutes ago about their kitchen layout. He described standing at the showroom floor mid-conversation and realising he had lost the thread entirely - not distracted, but genuinely unable to retrieve what had just been said. His manager had commented on it twice. A sale he had been close to finalising fell through after he failed to follow up correctly, and he was certain his colleagues had noticed the change in him, even if no one had named it directly.

At home, his partner had grown increasingly worried. Aleksander acknowledged that he had not been able to explain to her what was happening, partly because he did not fully understand it himself, and partly because he had come to believe - without quite deciding to - that naming it would make it more real.

What finally brought him in was a night three weeks ago when he sat awake until four in the morning, unable to explain to himself why he could not feel safe in his own apartment. His partner sat with him and said, gently, that she thought he needed to talk to someone. He is hoping, he said at the end of the intake, to feel like himself again. He is not entirely sure, he added, that he remembers what that was like.
